# Neuronal culture {#sec-culture}

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
import { stepper } from "./pedagogy/stepper.js"
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| output: false
// Growth rates reported by @dotti1988establishment (pp. 1455, 1457), used in the prose.
culAxonRate = 70      // µm/d, mean axonal rate over the first few days (p. 1457)
culDendRate = 12      // µm/d, dendrites between day 5 and day 7 (p. 1457)
culRatio = (culAxonRate / culDendRate).toFixed(1)
```

Nearly every number in this course was measured in a dish: the voltage-sensitive dye signals of @sec-indicators, the calcium transients of @sec-calcium, and the stiffness experiments of @sec-frontier, where neurons are grown on gels of chosen elastic modulus. Culture is also where the mechanical environment is easiest to set deliberately, by plating cells on a gel of chosen stiffness. This chapter is the minimum you need to read such a Methods section, and to plan your own.

::: {.callout-note title="After this chapter you will be able to"}
- describe the standard dissociated hippocampal culture and what it is used for;
- name the five stages by which a cultured neuron becomes polarised, with their approximate timings and growth rates;
- say what the substrate contributes, and why a thin soft gel does not feel soft;
- read a culture protocol and extract species, age, substrate, density and readout.
:::

## The standard preparation {#sec-culture-standard}

The reference protocol is still the one Dotti, Sullivan and Banker published in 1988 for **rat** embryonic day 18 (E18) hippocampus: hippocampi from 18-day rat fetuses, 0.25% trypsin for 15 min at 37 °C, trituration through a constricted Pasteur pipette, and 2,000–6,000 cells plated per dish on an acid-cleaned glass coverslip treated with polylysine [@dotti1988establishment, p. 1455]. Cells attach in minimal essential medium with 10% horse serum; after 3–4 h the medium is replaced by a serum-free one with HEPES, pyruvate and the N2 supplement. Survival is supported by a separate coverslip carrying a confluent astroglial monolayer, placed face-down above the neurons on a glass ring so that the two populations share medium without touching [@dotti1988establishment, p. 1455].

Two properties make this preparation the standard model of **neuronal polarity**, the division of a neuron into one axon and several dendrites. First, it is nearly pure: "about 90% of the neurons in hippocampal cultures are pyramidal cells; the rest are interneurons of several types", with few non-neuronal cells, and the cells survive "for a month or more" [@craig1994neuronal, p. 269]. Second, neurons polarise in culture without synapses or specific cell contacts, which argues that the program is endogenous [@craig1994neuronal, pp. 268–269]. Dotti and colleagues made the point directly by filming a neuron born by mitosis in the dish, with no contacts: within about 20 h after division both daughters had polarised [@dotti1988establishment, pp. 1460–1461].

## The five stages {#sec-culture-stages}

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| output: false
culStages = [
  {
    n: 1, day: "≈ 0.25 d",
    title: "Lamellipodia",
    text: "Shortly after the cells attach, motile lamellipodia — flat, veil-like structures, constantly in motion — develop around the periphery of the soma (Dotti et al. 1988, pp. 1457, 1461). Attachment itself happens in the first hour or two (p. 1457).",
    veil: true,
    processes: []
  },
  {
    n: 2, day: "≈ 0.5 d",
    title: "Minor processes",
    text: "The lamellipodia condense into several short 'minor processes', on average 4.9 per cell at 24 h (n = 17), each about 10 µm long and reaching 10–15 µm within a few hours, after which they stop elongating (Dotti et al. 1988, pp. 1455, 1457, 1461). None of them looks like an axon yet.",
    processes: [1, 1, 1, 1, 1]
  },
  {
    n: 3, day: "≈ 1.5 d",
    title: "Axonal outgrowth",
    text: "One minor process abruptly increases its rate of elongation almost 10-fold and can be identified as the axon within 2 h (Dotti et al. 1988, p. 1459). The cell is now polarised. Over 9 filmed cells this happened 8–30 h after plating (Table 1, p. 1459), and the axon reached about 40 µm by 1 day (p. 1457).",
    processes: [3.6, 1, 1, 1, 1]
  },
  {
    n: 4, day: "≈ 4 d",
    title: "Dendritic outgrowth",
    text: "The remaining minor processes begin to grow slowly into dendrites, about 12 µm/d between days 5 and 7, while the axon has been advancing at roughly 70 µm/d (Dotti et al. 1988, pp. 1455, 1457). The axon branches mainly by collaterals sprouting from the shaft behind the growth cone, seen in 16 of 19 cells (p. 1455).",
    processes: [5.2, 1.8, 1.8, 1.8, 1.8],
    collaterals: true
  },
  {
    n: 5, day: "> 7 d",
    title: "Maturation",
    text: "Dendrites become short, tapering, MAP2-positive processes while the axon stays long, thin and uniform; in the cell of their Fig. 1 the axon reached 300 µm and dendrites up to 75 µm by day 7 (Dotti et al. 1988, pp. 1454, 1455). Maturation 'continues for some weeks' (p. 1461).",
    processes: [6.4, 2.6, 2.6, 2.6, 2.6],
    collaterals: true,
    taper: true
  }
];
culAngles = [20, 150, 200, 255, 310];
culDraw = (st) => {
  const w = 460, h = 190, cx = 150, cy = 95, soma = 15, unit = 13;
  const parts = [];
  if (st.veil) {
    parts.push(`<circle cx="${cx}" cy="${cy}" r="${soma + 11}" fill="none" stroke="#eda100"
       stroke-width="2.5" stroke-dasharray="4 4" opacity="0.9"/>`);
    parts.push(`<text x="${cx + 32}" y="${cy - 26}" fill="#eda100" font-size="12">lamellipodia</text>`);
  }
  st.processes.forEach((len, i) => {
    const a = culAngles[i] * Math.PI / 180;
    const L = len * unit;
    const x1 = cx + Math.cos(a) * soma, y1 = cy - Math.sin(a) * soma;
    const x2 = cx + Math.cos(a) * (soma + L), y2 = cy - Math.sin(a) * (soma + L);
    const isAxon = i === 0 && st.n >= 3;
    const colour = isAxon ? "#eb6834" : (st.n >= 4 ? "#2a78d6" : "#9aa5b1");
    const wdt = isAxon ? 2.5 : (st.taper ? 4 : 2.5);
    parts.push(`<line x1="${x1}" y1="${y1}" x2="${x2}" y2="${y2}" stroke="${colour}"
       stroke-width="${wdt}" stroke-linecap="round"/>`);
    parts.push(`<circle cx="${x2}" cy="${y2}" r="${isAxon ? 4 : 2.5}" fill="${colour}"/>`);
    if (isAxon && st.collaterals) {
      [0.45, 0.7].forEach(f => {
        const bx = cx + Math.cos(a) * (soma + L * f), by = cy - Math.sin(a) * (soma + L * f);
        parts.push(`<line x1="${bx}" y1="${by}" x2="${bx + 14}" y2="${by - 22}"
           stroke="#eb6834" stroke-width="2"/>`);
      });
    }
  });
  parts.push(`<circle cx="${cx}" cy="${cy}" r="${soma}" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/>`);
  if (st.n >= 3) parts.push(`<text x="${cx + 60}" y="${cy + 30}" fill="#eb6834" font-size="12">axon</text>`);
  if (st.n >= 4) parts.push(`<text x="${cx - 120}" y="${cy - 30}" fill="#2a78d6" font-size="12">dendrites</text>`);
  parts.push(`<text x="8" y="18" fill="currentColor" font-size="13">Stage ${st.n}: ${st.title} (${st.day})</text>`);
  parts.push(`<text x="8" y="${h - 8}" fill="#9aa5b1" font-size="11">schematic, not to scale</text>`);
  const holder = document.createElement("div");
  holder.innerHTML = `<svg viewBox="0 0 ${w} ${h}" width="100%" style="max-width:460px"
     role="img" aria-label="Stage ${st.n}, ${st.title}">${parts.join("")}</svg>`;
  return holder.firstElementChild;
};
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof culStep = stepper(culStages, { delay: 2200 })
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| label: fig-polarity-stages
//| fig-cap: "Step through the five stages of polarisation of a dissociated rat E18 hippocampal neuron. Entry times are those given by Dotti et al. 1988 (Fig. 9, p. 1466): 0.25, 0.5, 1.5, 4 and more than 7 days in culture. Orange: the process that becomes the axon, with shaft collaterals from stage 4; blue: dendrites; grey: minor processes not yet specified; yellow dashed ring: lamellipodia. The drawings are schematic and not to scale — the axon and the minor processes differ by a factor of about 8 in length at 1–2 days (80–100 µm against 10–15 µm, p. 1455), far more than drawn."
html`<figure>${culDraw(culStep)}
<figcaption style="font-size:0.9em">${culStep.text}</figcaption></figure>`
```

The quantitative core of the sequence, shown stage by stage in @fig-polarity-stages, is the growth-rate difference. The axon of the cell in their Fig. 1 grew at about 60 µm/d, and averaged over 11 cells about ${culAxonRate} µm/d for the first few days, while dendrites elongated at about ${culDendRate} µm/d between days 5 and 7 — a factor of ${culRatio} here, quoted in the paper as 5–10 times [@dotti1988establishment, pp. 1455, 1457]. Per-cell time-lapse gives the same picture at finer grain: over the 18 h after the start of stage 3 the mean axonal rate was 6.3 µm/h, but the fastest 2 h interval of each cell averaged 20.3 µm/h [@dotti1988establishment, Table 1, p. 1459]. Growth is intermittent, not steady.

::: {.callout-warning title="Where the sources disagree"}
- *When dendrites start.* Fig. 9 and the Discussion give about 4 days; the legend of Fig. 4 says "after day 3"; the Results say "between days 3 and 5" [@dotti1988establishment, pp. 1457, 1459, 1464]. Quote the figure you rely on.
- *When the axon starts.* The text gives 8–27 h after plating, Table 1 on the same page lists 8–30 h [@dotti1988establishment, p. 1459].
- *How long minor processes are.* The primary paper gives 10–15 µm [@dotti1988establishment, p. 1455]; the review that popularised the stages gives "four to five short neurites, typically 15–25 µm in length" [@craig1994neuronal, p. 290]. Cite the primary numbers.
:::

## The substrate {#sec-culture-substrate}

Coatings are not neutral. Rat sympathetic neurons on polylysine alone, without glia or serum, make one axon and no dendrites; laminin increases the number of axons and the growth rate; Matrigel, "a basement membrane extract that contains a complex mixture of ECM proteins", induces dendrites [@craig1994neuronal, p. 296, Fig. 5]. In hippocampal neurons laminin raises the axonal growth rate but not the number of axons [@craig1994neuronal, p. 297]. And stickiness alone is not the point: "axon growth requires a physical substrate that is both adhesive and permissive for growth (many adhesive substrates fail to support axon growth)" [@tessierlavigne1996molecular, p. 1124].

For mechanics the coating sits on a gel whose stiffness you choose. Kreysing and colleagues cultured E17–E18 rat hippocampal neurons on hydroxy-polyacrylamide gels of shear elastic modulus about 0.1 kPa ("soft") and about 10 kPa ("stiff"), coated with 10–100 µg/ml poly-D-lysine overnight and then 1–2 µg/ml laminin for 4 h, and plated 150,000 cells per dish [@kreysing2025environmental, Methods, "Preparation and coating of hydrogels"; Methods, "Cell culture"]. The polyacrylamide recipe itself goes back to the gels Engler and colleagues used for stem cells, cast 70–100 µm thick and coated with 0.25–1 µg/cm² of collagen I [@engler2006matrix, p. 687].

::: {.callout-warning title="A thin soft gel is not soft"}
Cells feel roughly as deep as their adhesions reach. A gel only about 0.5–1 µm thick on glass "fosters cell spreading similar to that of cells on stiffer gels" [@engler2006matrix, p. 685]. If your gel is thin, your cells are on glass with a soft coat. Cast gels tens of micrometres thick and report the thickness.
:::

## Reading a protocol {#sec-culture-protocols}

Five things identify a culture: species, age, substrate, density and readout. The table collects the protocols used by the sources of this course; note that no two are the same, and that rat ages are never interchangeable with mouse ages.

| Species, age | Region / cell | Substrate | Density | Readout | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Rat, E18 | Hippocampus | Polylysine on glass + astroglial feeder coverslip | 2,000–6,000 per dish | Time-lapse morphology, MAP2 | @dotti1988establishment [p. 1455] |
| Rat, E17–E18 | Hippocampus | Polyacrylamide 0.1 or 10 kPa + PDL + laminin | 150,000 per dish | Patch clamp, Rhod-4 calcium, synapse staining | @kreysing2025environmental [Methods] |
| Rat, age not stated | Hippocampus | Matrigel, 24-well glass bottom | 225,000 viable cells per well | GCaMP screen with field stimulation | @chen2013ultrasensitive [Methods] |
| Rat, P0–P1 | Hippocampus | Poly-D-lysine on glass, NbActiv4, 8–10 DIV | not stated | Voltage imaging with Voltron (preprint) | @abdelfattah2019bright [Methods] |
| Mouse, newborn (P0) | Hippocampus | Poly-D-lysine, serum then Neurobasal/B27, 7–12 DIV | not stated | FMP voltage dye imaging | @fairless2013membrane [p. 2] |
| Mouse, adult | Dorsal root ganglia | Poly-L-lysine on glass, 7–12 DIV | not stated | FMP imaging, menthol and capsaicin | @fairless2013membrane [p. 2] |
| Mouse, E10.5 | Neural stem cells, neurospheres | Laminin-coated coverslips | 30,000 per cm² | Differentiation markers, proliferation | @nourse2022piezo [Methods] |

Three details in that table are worth copying into your own protocols. Chen and colleagues added 4 µM AraC to the growth medium to stop glia from proliferating, because a screen of neuronal fluorescence cannot afford a glial carpet [@chen2013ultrasensitive, Methods, "Neuronal culture screen"]. Nourse and colleagues grew mouse E10.5 neural stem cells as neurospheres with bFGF and EGF and then started differentiation by withdrawing the growth factors, scoring neurons and astrocytes at 4 days and oligodendrocytes at 10 days — timings set by the lineage, not by convenience [@nourse2022piezo, Methods]. And Fairless and colleagues imaged mouse hippocampal cultures only between 7 and 12 days in vitro, which is also when those neurons show the depolarising GABA responses of @sec-activity [@fairless2013membrane, p. 2; p. 10].

::: {.callout-note title="What culture cannot tell you" collapse="true"}
The authors of the stage model were careful about this. Lamellipodia of the kind seen in stage 1 "have not been observed in neurons developing in situ" and may reflect "adaptation to growth on an artificial, 2-dimensional substrate", and the relationship of minor processes to anything in the intact brain is uncertain [@dotti1988establishment, p. 1461]. The review makes the general version of the complaint: nearly all developmental work on polarity relies on culture, and how closely it parallels development in situ is unclear [@craig1994neuronal, p. 290].
:::

## Check yourself {#sec-culture-check}

:::{.qmulti}
In the Dotti staging, what marks the transition from stage 2 to stage 3?

- One of the minor processes abruptly grows much faster and becomes the axon.

  > Correct: an almost 10-fold rate increase, identifiable within 2 h [@dotti1988establishment, p. 1459].

- The cell attaches to the substrate and spreads lamellipodia.

  > That is the entry into stage 1, during the first hour or two [@dotti1988establishment, p. 1457].

- MAP2 becomes restricted to the dendrites.

  > MAP2 and tau are not differentially distributed when cells first polarise [@dotti1988establishment, p. 1466].

:::

**Compute.** An axon growing at the mean rate of @dotti1988establishment [p. 1457] for the first few days, 70 µm/d, is how many times faster than a dendrite at 12 µm/d? {{< qinput 5.8 tol=0.2 hints="70 ÷ 12" >}} [@dotti1988establishment, pp. 1455, 1457].

:::{.qmulti}
You cast 1 µm polyacrylamide gels of 0.1 kPa on glass and see no difference from glass controls. The most likely reason is…

- the cells sense the rigid glass through the thin gel.

  > Correct: a gel about 0.5–1 µm thick behaves like a stiff substrate [@engler2006matrix, p. 685].

- 0.1 kPa is too stiff to matter.

  > 0.1 kPa is at the soft end of the brain-like range used in these experiments [@kreysing2025environmental; @engler2006matrix].

:::

:::{.qmulti}
A paper reports "hippocampal neurons, E18, DIV 10". Which claim may you transfer to a mouse experiment at E18?

- None directly: E18 rat and E18 mouse are different developmental points, and the species must be stated with every claim.

  > Correct. Rat ages are not transferable to mouse; the sources of this course differ in both species and age [@dotti1988establishment; @fairless2013membrane].

- All of them, since both are rodents.

  > Gestation and developmental timing differ; the course convention is to label every biological claim with species and age.

:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Answers" collapse="true"}
1. One minor process starts growing much faster and becomes the axon [@dotti1988establishment, p. 1459].
2. 70 / 12 ≈ 5.8, consistent with the paper's "5–10 times" [@dotti1988establishment, p. 1457].
3. The cells feel the glass through the thin gel [@engler2006matrix, p. 685].
4. None; species and age go with every claim.
:::

## Summary {#sec-culture-summary}

- Dissociated rat E18 hippocampal culture on polylysine with an astroglial feeder is the standard polarity preparation: about 90% pyramidal neurons, viable for a month or more [@dotti1988establishment, p. 1455; @craig1994neuronal, p. 269].
- Polarisation runs through five stages entered at about 0.25, 0.5, 1.5, 4 and more than 7 days in culture [@dotti1988establishment, Fig. 9, p. 1466].
- The axon is defined by its growth rate: about 70 µm/d against about 12 µm/d for dendrites, 5–10 times faster, and it grows in bursts [@dotti1988establishment, pp. 1455, 1457, Table 1].
- The substrate changes the outcome: polylysine, laminin and Matrigel give different numbers of axons and dendrites, and adhesion alone is not sufficient for growth [@craig1994neuronal, p. 296; @tessierlavigne1996molecular, p. 1124].
- Stiffness experiments need gels thick enough to hide the glass; cells feel through a gel of about 0.5–1 µm [@engler2006matrix, p. 685], and brain-like gels of 0.1 and 10 kPa with PDL and laminin are the current standard for rat hippocampal neurons [@kreysing2025environmental, Methods].

:::{.qflashcards}

- Name the five stages of neuronal polarisation in culture.

  > Lamellipodia; minor processes; axonal outgrowth; dendritic outgrowth; maturation (entered at about 0.25, 0.5, 1.5, 4 and >7 days).

- What distinguishes the axon at stage 3?

  > Its rate: an abrupt, almost 10-fold increase in elongation, 5–10 times faster than the other processes.

- Why does gel thickness matter in a stiffness experiment?

  > Cells sense through a thin gel to the rigid glass below; around 0.5–1 µm a soft gel behaves stiff.

- Which five facts identify a culture protocol?

  > Species, age, substrate (and stiffness), plating density and readout.

:::
